text: Instagram's first background-task system was Gearman. As task volume grew to thousands per second, Instagram replaced it with Celery workers and a RabbitMQ broker, as described in a PyCon 2013 talk.
why: Corrects the year-one stack: Celery/RabbitMQ came after Gearman.

text: In 2010 Facebook served over 400 billion PHP page views a month, and built the HipHop PHP-to-C++ compiler to cut CPU use instead of leaving PHP.
why: Shows why Facebook kept PHP and how it scaled it.

text: S3 accepts a single PUT of up to 5 GB. Multipart upload sends parts independently, in any order and in parallel, and is meant for larger objects (5 MB to 50 TB).
why: Gives the threshold where chunked upload starts to make sense.

text: AWS does not charge for inbound data from the internet. S3 does not charge for transfer to AWS services in the same Region or to CloudFront. Data out to the internet, cross-AZ and cross-Region traffic is billed.
why: Lets readers work out which hops actually cost money.

text: A NAT gateway adds a per-GB data processing charge for traffic passing through it. A VPC gateway endpoint lets instances reach S3 in the same Region without data transfer charges.
why: A common hidden cost when servers in private subnets talk to S3.

text: A presigned POST policy can carry conditions such as content-length-range, Content-Type and acl. This lets the backend cap the upload size and restrict the file type even though it never sees the bytes.
why: Shows how direct uploads stay safe against oversized or wrong-type files.

text: AWS calls presigned URLs bearer tokens: anyone who has one can use it, repeatedly, until it expires. A bucket policy can reject signatures older than a limit (the s3:signatureAge condition).
why: Explains why expiries should be short and URLs protected.

text: A presigned URL can't outlive the credentials that signed it. SDK-signed URLs can last up to 7 days with an IAM user's keys, but URLs signed with temporary role credentials expire when the role session ends (EC2 instance role credentials last about 6 hours).
why: A common production surprise when URLs are signed on EC2/ECS.

text: New S3 buckets have ACLs disabled by default ('Bucket owner enforced'). Uploads that specify ACLs other than bucket-owner-full-control fail with 400 AccessControlListNotSupported. AWS recommends controlling access with bucket policies instead.
why: An acl=public-read upload like GitHub's would fail on a default bucket today.

text: With CloudFront origin access control, the bucket stays private. A bucket policy allows only the cloudfront.amazonaws.com service principal, for one specific distribution, to read objects.
why: The concrete way to make S3 reachable only through the CDN.

text: GCS signed URLs can be valid for at most 7 days, and anyone in possession of one can use it. Azure SAS tokens are generated client-side and are not tracked by Azure Storage; Microsoft recommends user delegation SAS, signed with Entra ID credentials.
why: Gives the cross-cloud equivalents concrete limits.

text: S3 Event Notifications can publish 'new object created' events to Lambda, SQS, SNS or EventBridge. Delivery is at-least-once and usually takes seconds, which is a natural trigger for asynchronous moderation of direct uploads.
why: Shows how moderation hooks into a direct-to-S3 upload flow.

text: S3 Lifecycle expiration actions delete objects on your behalf after a set age. Rules apply to a group of objects (for example a prefix used for not-yet-published uploads), so orphan cleanup needs no custom job.
why: A built-in alternative to a cleanup script.

text: By default, new S3 buckets, access points and objects don't allow public access. Block Public Access settings override bucket policies and ACLs that would make data public.
why: An open-for-writes bucket now has to be enabled deliberately.

text: GitHub limits image attachments to 10 MB. Since May 2023, new attachments in private and internal repositories can be viewed only by people with access to the repository; before that, anyone with the direct URL could view them.
why: Shows that public CDN URLs for uploads are a privacy decision.

text: Microsoft's guidance: many services use a hybrid. Some data goes through a front-end proxy that validates business rules, other data is written directly with a SAS. Data written directly should be validated before the application uses it.
